    Reading Sentinel-2 into pyramids¶

    pyramids-eo reads a Sentinel-2 product straight into a normal pyramids.Dataset through GDAL's bundled SENTINEL2 driver — no sentinelsat, rasterio, or SNAP. GDAL parses the .SAFE product structure, pyramids does the raster work, and pyramids_eo.sentinel adds the instrument semantics: which subdataset is which band, DN → reflectance, and scene-classification masking. Every call returns a plain pyramids Dataset, so crop, to_crs, plot, and to_file all work on the result.

    This notebook teaches the public entry points in pyramids_eo.sentinel:

    Function What it gives you
    open_product(path) a typed S2Product describing the scene
    from_sentinel2(path, bands=..., ...) selected bands → a single Dataset
    from_sentinel2(..., reflectance=True) DN read back as surface reflectance
    from_sentinel2(..., mask_scl=[...]) scene-classification masking

    By the end you'll read a true-colour composite, control bands and resolution, harmonise bands that live on different grids, and mask clouds with the scene-classification band.

    Prerequisite — a granule and credentials. We read a real Level-2A scene in place off the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem (CDSE) eodata S3 store — only the band windows we ask for are fetched, so there is no multi-GB download. That needs CDSE S3 keys in your environment: CDSE_S3_ACCESS_KEY and CDSE_S3_SECRET_KEY (create them at the CDSE S3 keys manager). To read a .SAFE you have downloaded locally instead, just point PRODUCT at its folder or .zip and skip the S3 setup.

    Setup¶

    Imports, and one helper that points GDAL's /vsis3 reader at CDSE's eodata store using the keys from your environment. (Reading a local .SAFE/.zip needs none of this.)

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    %matplotlib inline
import os
import warnings

import numpy as np
import pyramids  # noqa: F401  (activates the bundled GDAL/osgeo)
from osgeo import gdal

# Two benign internal warnings would otherwise clutter the output below.
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="Warning: 'partition' will ignore")
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="The no_data_value -9999 is out of range")

from pyramids_eo.sentinel import from_sentinel2, open_product
from pyramids_eo.sentinel.s2.masks import SclClass


def configure_cdse_s3():
    # Point GDAL's /vsis3 reader at CDSE eodata using the CDSE_S3_* env keys.
    for key, value in {
        "AWS_S3_ENDPOINT": "eodata.dataspace.copernicus.eu",
        "AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID": os.environ.get("CDSE_S3_ACCESS_KEY", ""),
        "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY": os.environ.get("CDSE_S3_SECRET_KEY", ""),
        "AWS_VIRTUAL_HOSTING": "FALSE",
        "AWS_HTTPS": "YES",
        "GDAL_DISABLE_READDIR_ON_OPEN": "EMPTY_DIR",
    }.items():
        gdal.SetConfigOption(key, value)


configure_cdse_s3()
    %matplotlib inline import os import warnings import numpy as np import pyramids # noqa: F401 (activates the bundled GDAL/osgeo) from osgeo import gdal # Two benign internal warnings would otherwise clutter the output below. warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="Warning: 'partition' will ignore") warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="The no_data_value -9999 is out of range") from pyramids_eo.sentinel import from_sentinel2, open_product from pyramids_eo.sentinel.s2.masks import SclClass def configure_cdse_s3(): # Point GDAL's /vsis3 reader at CDSE eodata using the CDSE_S3_* env keys. for key, value in { "AWS_S3_ENDPOINT": "eodata.dataspace.copernicus.eu", "AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID": os.environ.get("CDSE_S3_ACCESS_KEY", ""), "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY": os.environ.get("CDSE_S3_SECRET_KEY", ""), "AWS_VIRTUAL_HOSTING": "FALSE", "AWS_HTTPS": "YES", "GDAL_DISABLE_READDIR_ON_OPEN": "EMPTY_DIR", }.items(): gdal.SetConfigOption(key, value) configure_cdse_s3()

    Our scene is a cloud-free Level-2A tile over Madrid (20 Aug 2024, tile T30TVK). PRODUCT is the path GDAL opens — the product's MTD_MSIL2A.xml inside the .SAFE, here on CDSE's S3 store. AOI is a small ~3 km window in the tile's native UTM CRS (EPSG:32630); keeping the read window small keeps every cell fast.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    PRODUCT = (
    "/vsis3/eodata/Sentinel-2/MSI/L2A/2024/08/20/"
    "S2A_MSIL2A_20240820T105621_N0511_R094_T30TVK_20240820T152852.SAFE/MTD_MSIL2A.xml"
)
AOI = (440000, 4470000, 443000, 4473000)  # (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) in EPSG:32630
    PRODUCT = ( "/vsis3/eodata/Sentinel-2/MSI/L2A/2024/08/20/" "S2A_MSIL2A_20240820T105621_N0511_R094_T30TVK_20240820T152852.SAFE/MTD_MSIL2A.xml" ) AOI = (440000, 4470000, 443000, 4473000) # (minx, miny, maxx, maxy) in EPSG:32630

    The product model¶

    open_product sniffs the driver and returns a typed S2Product — the level, the DN → reflectance quantification value, the native resolutions present (10 / 20 / 60 m), the UTM zone, and the band catalogue. Nothing is read yet; this is just the manifest.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    product = open_product(PRODUCT)
print("level:        ", product.level)
print("quantification:", product.quantification)
print("resolutions:  ", product.resolutions, "m")
print("UTM EPSG:     ", product.epsg_codes)
print("baseline:     ", product.baseline)
sorted(product.available_bands)
    product = open_product(PRODUCT) print("level: ", product.level) print("quantification:", product.quantification) print("resolutions: ", product.resolutions, "m") print("UTM EPSG: ", product.epsg_codes) print("baseline: ", product.baseline) sorted(product.available_bands)

UTM EPSG:      [32630]
baseline:      05.11

    True-colour reflectance¶

    from_sentinel2 selects bands by name and returns a Dataset. With reflectance=True (the default), the DN → reflectance conversion is recorded as lazy GDAL scale/offset tags rather than a materialised float array — the values become reflectance only when you read with read_array(scaled=True), and the tags survive crop/reproject.

    Here: red/green/blue (B04/B03/B02, all 10 m) over the AOI, rendered with the Dataset's built-in percentile-stretched RGB plot.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    rgb = from_sentinel2(PRODUCT, bands=["B04", "B03", "B02"], bbox=AOI)
print("shape:", rgb.shape, "| epsg:", rgb.epsg, "| cell:", rgb.cell_size, "m")
rgb.plot(
    rgb_options={"rgb": [0, 1, 2], "percentile": 2},
    title="Sentinel-2 true colour (B04/B03/B02)",
)
    rgb = from_sentinel2(PRODUCT, bands=["B04", "B03", "B02"], bbox=AOI) print("shape:", rgb.shape, "| epsg:", rgb.epsg, "| cell:", rgb.cell_size, "m") rgb.plot( rgb_options={"rgb": [0, 1, 2], "percentile": 2}, title="Sentinel-2 true colour (B04/B03/B02)", )
    shape: (3, 300, 300) | epsg: 32630 | cell: 10.0 m
    Out[4]:
    <cleopatra.glyphs.gridded.array_glyph.ArrayGlyph at 0x239578517f0>

    The scale/offset tags are what make a scaled read return physical reflectance. This is a baseline-≥04.00 product, so it carries the −1000 radiometric offset: reflectance = (DN − 1000) / 10000. Read both ways to see it:

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    print("scale :", rgb.scale)
print("offset:", rgb.offset)
scaled = np.asarray(rgb.read_array(scaled=True), dtype="float64")
print(
    "reflectance min / mean / max:",
    round(float(np.nanmin(scaled)), 3),
    round(float(np.nanmean(scaled)), 3),
    round(float(np.nanmax(scaled)), 3),
)
    print("scale :", rgb.scale) print("offset:", rgb.offset) scaled = np.asarray(rgb.read_array(scaled=True), dtype="float64") print( "reflectance min / mean / max:", round(float(np.nanmin(scaled)), 3), round(float(np.nanmean(scaled)), 3), round(float(np.nanmax(scaled)), 3), )
    scale : [0.0001, 0.0001, 0.0001]
offset: [-0.1, -0.1, -0.1]
reflectance min / mean / max: 0.009 0.136 0.691

    A single band with a colour map¶

    Any band works the same way. The near-infrared B08 (10 m) is high over vegetation and low over built-up land and water — the basis of indices like NDVI.

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    nir = from_sentinel2(PRODUCT, bands=["B08"], bbox=AOI)
nir.plot(band=0, title="Sentinel-2 near-infrared (B08) reflectance", cmap="RdYlGn")
    nir = from_sentinel2(PRODUCT, bands=["B08"], bbox=AOI) nir.plot(band=0, title="Sentinel-2 near-infrared (B08) reflectance", cmap="RdYlGn")
    Out[6]:
    <cleopatra.glyphs.gridded.array_glyph.ArrayGlyph at 0x23959caf4d0>

    Cross-resolution harmonise¶

    Sentinel-2 bands live on different grids: B04 is 10 m, the SWIR B11 is 20 m. Ask for both and from_sentinel2 reads each at its native resolution and harmonises them onto the finest grid — here 10 m — so they stack into one aligned Dataset you can index band-by-band.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    stack = from_sentinel2(PRODUCT, bands=["B04", "B11"], bbox=AOI)
print("bands:", stack.band_count, "| cell:", stack.cell_size, "m | shape:", stack.shape)
stack.plot(band=1, title="SWIR B11 (20 m) resampled onto the 10 m grid", cmap="magma")
    stack = from_sentinel2(PRODUCT, bands=["B04", "B11"], bbox=AOI) print("bands:", stack.band_count, "| cell:", stack.cell_size, "m | shape:", stack.shape) stack.plot(band=1, title="SWIR B11 (20 m) resampled onto the 10 m grid", cmap="magma")
    bands: 2 | cell: 10.0 m | shape: (2, 300, 300)
    Out[7]:
    <cleopatra.glyphs.gridded.array_glyph.ArrayGlyph at 0x2395b033890>

    Scene-classification masking¶

    Level-2A ships a Scene Classification (SCL) band that labels every pixel — vegetation, water, bare soil, cloud, cloud shadow, snow. SclClass names those codes. Read the SCL band and plot the classification map:

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    scl = from_sentinel2(PRODUCT, bands=["SCL"], bbox=AOI)
codes = np.asarray(scl.read_array())
present = sorted(int(c) for c in np.unique(codes))
print("SCL classes present:", [SclClass(c).name for c in present])
scl.plot(band=0, title="Scene classification (SCL codes)", cmap="tab20")
    scl = from_sentinel2(PRODUCT, bands=["SCL"], bbox=AOI) codes = np.asarray(scl.read_array()) present = sorted(int(c) for c in np.unique(codes)) print("SCL classes present:", [SclClass(c).name for c in present]) scl.plot(band=0, title="Scene classification (SCL codes)", cmap="tab20")
    SCL classes present: ['DARK_FEATURE_SHADOW', 'VEGETATION', 'BARE_SOIL_DESERT', 'WATER']
    Out[8]:
    <cleopatra.glyphs.gridded.array_glyph.ArrayGlyph at 0x2395b0cd0f0>

    Pass mask_scl= to from_sentinel2 and the listed classes are set to no-data across every band. In practice you would usually mask the cloud and cloud-shadow classes, but this scene is cloud-free — so to make the effect obvious we mask everything that isn't vegetation (bare soil, water, and shadow), leaving a vegetation-only view of the near-infrared band:

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    non_vegetation = [
    SclClass.BARE_SOIL_DESERT,
    SclClass.WATER,
    SclClass.DARK_FEATURE_SHADOW,
]
masked = from_sentinel2(PRODUCT, bands=["B08"], bbox=AOI, mask_scl=non_vegetation)
nodata = masked.no_data_value[0]
changed = int(np.count_nonzero(np.asarray(masked.read_array()) == nodata))
print(f"pixels masked to no-data ({nodata}):", changed)
masked.plot(
    band=0, title="B08 with non-vegetation SCL classes masked out", cmap="RdYlGn"
)
    non_vegetation = [ SclClass.BARE_SOIL_DESERT, SclClass.WATER, SclClass.DARK_FEATURE_SHADOW, ] masked = from_sentinel2(PRODUCT, bands=["B08"], bbox=AOI, mask_scl=non_vegetation) nodata = masked.no_data_value[0] changed = int(np.count_nonzero(np.asarray(masked.read_array()) == nodata)) print(f"pixels masked to no-data ({nodata}):", changed) masked.plot( band=0, title="B08 with non-vegetation SCL classes masked out", cmap="RdYlGn" )
    pixels masked to no-data (0.0): 79192
    Out[9]:
    <cleopatra.glyphs.gridded.array_glyph.ArrayGlyph at 0x2395b0cce90>

    Takeaway¶

    You can now read Sentinel-2 into pyramids with:

    • open_product(path) for the typed S2Product manifest;
    • from_sentinel2(path, bands=..., bbox=..., reflectance=True) for an aligned, reflectance-tagged Dataset;
    • band names that harmonise across the 10 / 20 / 60 m grids automatically;
    • mask_scl=[SclClass...] for scene-classification masking.

    Everything returns a standard pyramids Dataset, so from here you'd continue with to_crs, crop, to_file (GeoTIFF/COG), and the rest of pyramids. For a time series, collection_from_sentinel2([...], root_dir=...) writes one GeoTIFF per scene and hands back a DatasetCollection.
